title: The Double Bind: Why Wholesale Distributors Run Short on Cash Right Before Their Biggest Quarter
linkedin:
Most wholesale and distribution businesses are having their best month of the year right now, and their tightest cash position at the same time.

Here's why. To be ready for the Christmas order cycle, distributors need stock on the shelf weeks before the first purchase order lands, which means buying now, often well above the usual monthly run rate.

At the same time, the retailers placing those big orders are managing their own cash. Many ask for sixty or ninety day terms instead of the usual thirty, because they don't want to pay for stock before it sells. Most distributors say yes, because turning down a large seasonal order over payment terms feels like the wrong fight to pick in August.

The result is a double bind. Cash goes out earlier to fund the stock build. Cash comes in later because the terms attached to that stock have stretched. Both sides of the working capital equation move against the business in the same eight week window, right when the dollar value moving through it is at its highest.

The businesses that handle this well treat the stock build and the terms conversation as one decision made now, not two decisions made separately as they come up. That means staging inventory around confirmed orders, holding the line on terms for smaller accounts, and asking for a deposit on the very large ones.

A note for wholesale and distribution business owners across Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria who are starting to build stock for the Christmas order cycle.

This is often the tightest cash stretch of the year, even though it looks like the strongest quarter on paper. Stock needs to be bought and paid for weeks before it sells, and at the same time many of the retail customers placing big Christmas orders ask for longer payment terms so they aren't paying before their own stock moves. Both changes land in the same few weeks, which stretches how long cash is tied up right when the dollar amounts involved are at their highest for the year.

The businesses that manage this well treat the stock build and the payment terms conversation as one decision made in August, rather than two separate decisions made as they come up. That usually means staging orders around confirmed demand, being selective about who gets extended terms, and checking early whether the existing cash buffer or bank facility genuinely covers the gap.

If this pattern sounds familiar as you head into your own Christmas stock build, it is worth working through before the orders start landing rather than after. Read the full piece on the blog.
